BST260 Final Project Proposal

Hongyu Li

Source: vignettes/proposal.qmd

To: BST260 Teaching Team, Fall 2026

Project overview

I propose two exploratory analyses using datasets listed in the BST260 project instructions: the NHANES data from the NHANES R package and the CDC foodborne and waterborne outbreak data included in this project as waterborne. Each analysis will have its own vignette, research question, descriptive summaries, figures, and discussion of limitations.

Analysis 1: BMI and systolic blood pressure in adults aged 40 and older

Research question: Among adults aged 40 years and older in the 2009–2012 NHANES educational dataset, how is body mass index associated with average systolic blood pressure?

Data and population. I will use NHANES::NHANES, an educational dataset derived from the National Center for Health Statistics’ 2009–2010 and 2011–2012 National Health and Nutrition Examination Surveys. Its source and variable definitions are documented in the NHANES package and the CDC NHANES website. The unit of analysis is a participant record in the resampled educational dataset; the analysis will include records with Age >= 40. The dataset samples participant records with replacement, so some participant IDs appear more than once. I will retain the educational sample as supplied and describe that resampling when interpreting the results.

Exposure and outcome. The exposure is BMI in kg/m², analyzed as a continuous variable, with the association reported per 5 kg/m². The outcome is BPSysAve, average systolic blood pressure in mm Hg, also continuous. I will exclude records with missing BMI, blood pressure, or prespecified adjustment variables from the adjusted model, report missingness and the number excluded, and compare basic characteristics of included and excluded records where possible. Missing values will not be coded as zero.

Analysis plan. Before examining associations, I will prespecify age (Age, continuous), sex (Gender), and race/ethnicity (Race1) as adjustment variables because they may relate to both BMI and blood pressure. I will summarize participant characteristics, BMI and blood pressure using counts, percentages, medians and interquartile ranges, and display a scatterplot with a smooth trend. I will fit an unadjusted and an adjusted linear regression, report estimates and 95% confidence intervals, inspect residuals and the shape of the BMI association, and describe exploratory age and sex interactions if sample sizes permit. The resampled data and cross-sectional design limit precision and causal interpretation; the package describes this dataset as adapted for teaching, not a research database. Results will be presented as exploratory associations, not definitive population estimates.

Analysis 2: Water exposure and reported outbreak size

Research question: Among reported U.S. waterborne disease outbreaks in the project’s CDC dataset, how does the number of reported illnesses differ between drinking-water and treated recreational-water outbreaks?

Data and population. I will use data("waterborne", package = "finalproject"), the CDC outbreak data supplied with the course template; its documented source is the CDC data API. The dataset contains outbreaks with multiple transmission modes, so I will restrict this analysis to records with primary_mode equal to Water. The unit of analysis is one reported outbreak, not one person. The analysis population is the subset of these records with exactly one of the two selected water exposure categories.

Exposure and outcome. The exposure is water_exposure, coded as Drinking water or Recreational water -- treated; outbreaks with multiple listed exposure types, other categories, or missing exposure will be excluded from the main comparison and counted separately. The outcome is illnesses, a nonnegative count of reported illnesses per outbreak. I will parse it as numeric, treat missing or invalid values as missing rather than zero, and report exclusions and missingness. These counts describe outbreak size, not infection risk or incidence rates.

Analysis plan. I will summarize counts of eligible outbreaks and the median and interquartile range of reported illnesses by exposure, and plot the distribution on a log-scaled axis where appropriate. Before comparing outcomes, I will choose outbreak year (year) and state (state) as adjustment variables: differences in time and location may affect exposure patterns, surveillance, and outbreak reporting. I will inspect category sizes and missingness first; if the data support it, I will fit a negative binomial regression for illness counts with exposure, year, and state, reporting the adjusted ratio of expected reported illnesses with a 95% confidence interval. If the model is unstable, I will report the descriptive comparison and explain why rather than present unreliable estimates. Differences in investigation, reporting, outbreak setting, pathogen, and the number of people exposed can confound the comparison; the data lack a common population-at-risk denominator. Therefore, I will not interpret the results as causal effects or population incidence.

Deliverables

The final site will include two reproducible analysis vignettes with data provenance, descriptive statistics, visualizations, methods, findings, uncertainty, and limitations. The proposal states intended analyses; it does not claim results before they have been calculated.
